statement: The transpose of an m x n matrix A, written A^T, is the n x m matrix obtained by swapping A's row and column indices: [A^T]_{ij} = [A]_{ji}. The source presents the standard algebraic identities of this operation as properties that follow from the definition, listing them without individual step-by-step proofs. The one exception is the symmetry of AA^T (and A^TA), for which the source gives an explicit short derivation by chaining two of the other identities: (AA^T)^T = (A^T)^T A^T = AA^T.

symbols.meaning: matrix, conformable with A for the stated operation
symbols.dimensions: m x n (add/scalar) or n x p (product AB)

symbols.meaning: column vectors used in the dot-product identities
entry (i,j) of the product AA^T, used in the source's index argument for symmetry

properties.why: stated directly as a property of the definition

properties.property: Additivity: (A + B)^T = A^T + B^T. 'The transpose respects addition.'
properties.why: stated directly as a property of the definition

properties.property: Scalar factor: (cA)^T = c(A^T). Combined with additivity, this makes transpose a linear map from m x n matrices to n x m matrices.
properties.why: stated directly, with the linearity conclusion given explicitly in the source

properties.property: Product reversal: (AB)^T = B^T A^T; the order of factors reverses. By induction this extends to (A1 A2 ... Ak)^T = Ak^T ... A2^T A1^T.
properties.why: stated directly, with the multi-factor extension attributed to induction

properties.property: Determinant invariance: det(A^T) = det(A) for a square matrix.
properties.why: stated directly as a property of the definition

properties.property: Dot product as matrix product: a . b = a^T b for column vectors a, b.
properties.why: stated directly; used again in the adjoint identity below

properties.property: If A has only real entries, A^T A is positive-semidefinite.
properties.why: stated directly as a property of the definition

properties.property: Inverse-transpose commute: (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T, so the transpose of an invertible matrix is invertible, with inverse equal to the transpose of the inverse.
properties.why: stated directly as a property of the definition

properties.property: A and A^T share the same characteristic polynomial, hence the same eigenvalues.
properties.why: stated directly ('their eigenvalues are equal ... since they share the same characteristic polynomial')

properties.property: Adjoint-style identity: (Aa) . b = a . (A^T b) for column vectors a, b and the standard dot product.
properties.why: stated directly as a property of the definition

properties.property: AA^T and A^T A are symmetric matrices.
properties.why: the source gives an explicit derivation: entrywise, p_ij = p_ji because both are obtained as the inner product of rows i and j of A, and separately a 'quick proof' shows (AA^T)^T = (A^T)^T A^T = AA^T by applying the product-reversal identity then the involution identity

assumptions.assumption: Matrix dimensions are conformable for the stated operation (e.g. A and B same shape for addition, A's columns match B's rows for the product AB).
assumptions.breaks_when: shapes are mismatched, in which case the operation is undefined

assumptions.assumption: The positive-semidefinite property of A^T A requires A to have real entries.
assumptions.breaks_when: A has complex entries; the source's complex analogues (Hermitian, unitary) use the conjugate transpose instead of the plain transpose

assumptions.assumption: The inverse-transpose identity (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T requires A to be invertible.
assumptions.breaks_when: A is singular, so A^{-1} does not exist

assumptions.assumption: The eigenvalue/characteristic-polynomial and similarity-to-A^T claims are stated for square matrices.
assumptions.breaks_when: A is not square, since eigenvalues and similarity are undefined

failure_modes.mode: Applying (AB)^T = A^T B^T instead of B^T A^T
failure_modes.signature: computed transpose has wrong shape or wrong numerical entries whenever A, B do not commute
failure_modes.cause: forgetting that the product-reversal identity swaps the order of the factors

failure_modes.mode: Assuming A^T A is positive-semidefinite for complex A
failure_modes.signature: x^T (A^T A) x can be non-real or negative for complex A
failure_modes.cause: the PSD property in the source is stated only for real-entry A; complex matrices need the conjugate transpose (Hermitian) version

failure_modes.mode: Treating the transpose and the adjoint as identical in a non-orthonormal basis
failure_modes.signature: matrix representing the adjoint of a linear map does not equal A^T
failure_modes.cause: the source notes the adjoint's matrix equals the transpose only when bases are orthonormal with respect to the relevant bilinear forms
